Quarto: one source for reports, papers and slides

The problem it solves

Results get scattered. The analysis is in one place, the text in a Word file, the slides in PowerPoint, and the numbers in between were copied by hand, so they are out of date the moment the data changes. Academic writing adds citations, cross-references and equations on top, and at work I just need a clean report by tomorrow.

The general idea

Quarto is an open-source publishing system from Posit. You write Markdown with code chunks (Python, R or Julia), and one source renders to HTML, PDF, Word, ePub, slides, websites and books. It is built on Pandoc and runs the code with Jupyter or knitr, so tables and figures in the document come straight from the analysis and are rebuilt every time. It is where R Markdown went, in one consistent system. It is the best tool I know for writing and reporting results.

## Method

We estimate the effect of rooms on price.

```{python}
plot(df)
```
quarto render report.qmd                 # HTML
quarto render report.qmd --to docx       # Word
quarto preview report.qmd                # live preview while writing

Tips from my setup

  • The same tool at work and in academia. A quick report for colleagues, a paper draft with citations and cross-references, and a conference deck all start from a .qmd file.
  • Slides as code. My conference slides are Quarto revealjs decks, and a coding-agent skill knows how to build and tidy them. Plain text means the slides diff, version and rebuild like any other code.
  • Websites and courses. This website, and the site of my Big Data course, were Quarto projects, built from the same plain-text posts.
  • In the editor. quarto-nvim runs the code chunks and gives language support inside them, so I write documents in Neovim like any other code.
  • Keep the analysis outside. The heavy work lives in scripts and DuckDB. The document loads the results and shows them, so rendering is fast.
